body.text: Few places or corridors tell a richer story of geography and human movement than Orlando International Airport. Stepping into its history reveals how trade, terrain, and culture shaped the modern map.

The airport code MCO comes from the airport's former name, McCoy Air Force Base, a Strategic Air Command installation, that was closed in 1975 as part of a general military drawdown following the end of the Vietnam War.

The airport serves as an operating base for Breeze Airways, Frontier Airlines, and Southwest Airlines as well as a focus city for JetBlue. Southwest is the airport's largest carrier by passengers carried.

The airport is also a major international gateway for the Florida region, with over 1,000 daily flights on more than 40 airlines serving over 170 domestic and international destinations. 0 km2), MCO is one of the largest commercial airports in terms of land area in the United States.
In addition, the airport is home to a maintenance base for United Airlines. The airport was also a hub for Delta Air Lines until 2007.
History
Military years

The airfield originated during World War II as a United States Army Air Forces facility. In 1942, the Army acquired land southeast of Orlando to develop an airfield for military aviation operations, including those of the Boeing B-17 Flying Fortress.

Originally known as Orlando Army Air Field Number Two, the installation served as an auxiliary airfield to Orlando Army Air Base, now known as Orlando Executive Airport. It was renamed Pinecastle Army Airfield in 1943.

Following World War II, Pinecastle was used for early flight testing of the Bell X-1 experimental aircraft. On January 19, 1946, Bell test pilot Jack Woolams conducted the aircraft's first unpowered glide flight after being released from a Boeing B-29 Superfortress.

Woolams completed ten glide flights before the aircraft was returned to Bell for installation of its rocket engine. The X-1 program subsequently continued at Muroc Army Airfield in California, now Edwards Air Force Base, where Chuck Yeager achieved the first supersonic flight on October 14, 1947.

After the war, the airfield was decommissioned, and most of its facilities were dismantled. The property was deeded back to the City of Orlando in 1948. In 1951, during the Korean War, the installation was reactivated as Pinecastle Air Force Base to serve as a training facility for Boeing B-47 Stratojet bombers.
It became a combat facility under the Strategic Air Command (SAC) in 1954.

The 321st Bombardment Wing was activated at Pinecastle on December 15, 1953, and operated B-47 Stratojet bombers and Boeing KC-97 Stratofreighter aerial refueling aircraft. Colonel Michael Norman Wright McCoy assumed command of the wing in 1954.

On October 9, 1957, McCoy was killed when his B-47 Stratojet crashed north of Orlando during a flight demonstration. The crash also killed the other three occupants of the aircraft, including an officer of the British Royal Air Force.
Pinecastle Air Force Base was renamed McCoy Air Force Base in May 1958 in honor of the colonel.

In the early 1960s, McCoy transitioned from medium bomber operations to heavy bomber operations. The introduction of the Boeing B-52 Stratofortress in 1961 resulted in the construction of two parallel runways approximately 12,000 feet (3,700 m) in length.
On April 1, 1963, the 306th Bombardment Wing relocated from MacDill Air Force Base to McCoy, where it operated B-52 bombers and Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling aircraft.

McCoy also hosted the 966th Airborne Early Warning and Control Squadron, a unit of the Air Defense Command, from February 1962 to December 1969. The squadron conducted airborne radar surveillance using RC-121 and Lockheed EC-121 Warning Star aircraft.
During the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962, McCoy Air Force Base became a forward operating location for tactical fighter aircraft.

As part of the United States military buildup in Florida, the Strategic Air Command dispersed bomber and tanker aircraft from McCoy and other Florida bases to make room for aircraft of the Tactical Air Command.

The forces deployed to McCoy included Republic F-105 Thunderchief fighter-bombers of the 4th Tactical Fighter Wing and North American F-100 Super Sabre fighter-bombers of the 354th Tactical Fighter Wing.

McCoy also served as a base for Lockheed U-2 reconnaissance flights over Cuba. On October 27, 1962, Major Rudolf Anderson Jr. was killed when his U-2, which had departed McCoy on a reconnaissance mission, was shot down over Cuba by a Soviet SA-2 Guideline surface-to-air missile. Anderson was posthumously awarded the first Air Force Cross.
In 1973, the United States Department of Defense announced plans to close McCoy Air Force Base as part of a broader reduction and realignment of military installations.

The closure plan called for the inactivation of the 306th Bombardment Wing and its B-52D-equipped 36th Bombardment Squadron, the reassignment of KC-135 aircraft to McConnell Air Force Base and Lockbourne Air Force Base, and the relocation of an EC-121 detachment of the 55th Airborne Early Warning and Control Squadron to Homestead Air Force Base.

The 306th Bombardment Wing was inactivated on July 1, 1974, ending its operations at McCoy. Following the closure of the military base in 1974, the City of Orlando received the deed to surplus airport property in 1975. Most of the former military installation subsequently became part of Orlando International Airport.
Civil-military years

The introduction of commercial jet aircraft in the late 1950s and early 1960s created a need for longer runways than those available at Orlando's existing commercial airport, now known as Orlando Executive Airport.

The introduction of B-52 bombers at McCoy Air Force Base in 1961 led to the construction of two parallel runways approximately 12,000 feet (3,700 m) in length, making the installation suitable for commercial jet operations.

In 1962, the City of Orlando and the United States Air Force entered into a joint-use agreement that allocated approximately 960 acres (390 ha) for civilian aviation facilities. The Air Force permitted commercial aircraft to use Runway 18L/36R, and civilian terminal facilities were developed alongside the existing military installation.

The city subsequently acquired additional land for civilian aviation development and completed its first airport master plan in 1969, establishing the framework for the expansion of the commercial airport.

The 1971 opening of Magic Kingdom at Walt Disney World led to a significant increase in air travel as Orlando became a major tourist destination. For much of the 1970s, Shawnee Airlines would directly link MCO with Walt Disney World using de Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter commuter aircraft.

These connecting flights flew from MCO to the Walt Disney World STOL Airport, a small, short-lived airfield near the Magic Kingdom's parking lot. Deregulation of the airline industry in 1978 also contributed to increases in air service to Orlando.

When McCoy AFB closed in 1975, part of the facility stayed under military control to support Naval Training Center Orlando and several tenant commands until NTC Orlando was closed in 1999 pursuant to a post-Cold War 1993 BRAC Commission decision.

There are only a few enclaves on the original McCoy AFB site that the military still uses such as the 164th Air Defense Artillery Brigade from the Florida Army National Guard in the former McCoy AFB Officers Club complex, an Army Reserve intelligence unit in the former SAC Alert Facility, the 1st Lieutenant David R.

Wilson Armed Forces Reserve Center supporting multiple units of the Army Reserve, Navy Reserve and Marine Corps Reserve that was constructed in 2002, and a large Navy Exchange for active, reserve and retired military personnel and their dependents.
Civil years

In 1975, following the closure of McCoy Air Force Base, the City of Orlando received the airport property from the federal government. The Greater Orlando Aviation Authority (GOAA) was established by an act of the Florida Legislature that year to manage and develop the city's airports, including Orlando Executive Airport.
In 1976, the airport received international status and was renamed Orlando International Airport, retaining the airport code MCO derived from its former military designation.
